old_title: Quick hits: Das's redemption and Mehid's Messi attempt
new_title: Quick hits: Das's redemption and Mehid's Messi attempt
old_text:
Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them, as Mitch Starc's desperate review spoke volumes and Cameron Green's redemptive arc proved to be in vain.
- As it happened: Bangladesh beats Australia by nine wickets
Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test, as Bangladesh claimed a stunning victory, their first ever in a Test on Australian soil.
1. Das's day four redemption
Australia began the day still 67 runs in arrears, knowing that any early slip-ups could prove fatal to their hopes of pulling off an unlikely escape.
So, Alex Carey's heart was surely in his mouth as the excellent Hasan Mahmud had him edging during the fourth over of the day.
It was a tough chance, but one experienced Bangladeshi wicketkeeper Litton Das would have been hopeful of gobbling up.
Das was too slow to react, and the ball flew past his outstretched left glove and to the boundary.
But Carey was unable to profit from that early slice of fortune, finding himself walking back to the pavilion just three overs later.
This time, Das made no mistake with what, probably, was a more difficult chance, with Carey feathering one through off the bowling of spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz.
It was a superb delivery from Mehidy, pitching and gripping and turning away from the Australian wicketkeeper.
Das had his redemption and Bangladesh was on its way.
2. Webster falls to a beauty
Spin bowling is an art form built on deception, with guile and sleight of hand as important as pin-point accuracy.
On a pitch offering few surprises and only the minimum of turn, it is the impetus of a genuine spinner to trick their way into the minds of their rivals.
Beau Webster had played sensibly through the first 20 balls of his innings, alert to the threat of Mehidy Hasan Miraz's off spinners.
Mehidy was probing at the off stump of Webster, but the ball that deceived him was simply wonderful.
Angling the ball so that the seam would not bite, Mehidy just pushed the ball through a couple of kilometres per hour faster than the balls before.
With no seam to grip, the ball skidded on, perhaps a little lower, and took the top of his off stump.
A master magician couldn't have disguised his intents better and Australia's tail was exposed.
3. Starc's desperate review
Australia began the second session with a 15-run lead and just three wickets in hand, requiring something very special from both Cam Green and Mitch Starc.
So, when Starc nicked off in the third over after lunch, the final nail was well and truly closing in on the Australian coffin.
There was a clear noise and a dramatic deviation, but Starc, well aware of the value of his wicket, decided to send the call upstairs.
Unlike Steve Smith on day three, who had so defiantly called for a review even before Kumar Dharmasena had raised his finger, Starc questioned this decision with embarrassment.
He began his walk from the middle with the review still underway.
There were no ghosts in the machine, no undetected front foot no ball, and Australia was in touching distance of a chastening defeat.
4. Mehidy's footwork lets him down
Given the magic that had been cascading from Mehidy's right hand all day, you wouldn't have put it past the off spinner from doing something special with his foot.
But Mehidy was more messy than Messi when presented with opportunity.
Nathan Lyon, new to crease, was slow to take off for a single, and there was a real chance of a run out, with a Bangladeshi fielder circling in the infield.
But the throw was off target, and Mehidy was forced to improvise, attempting to sidefoot the wayward effort towards the pegs.
Instead, the ball thudded into his ankle and fell limply to earth, Mehidy wincing as he returned to his mark.
It looked like a really painful one, but, thankfully, he was right to continue.
5. Green's drought-breaking ton
Having not passed 50 in his previous 13 Test innings, Cameron Green's position in the side was very much a topic of conversation heading into this Test.
A jittery run-a-ball 13 in the first innings would have done little but amplify those calls for him to be replaced.
But on days three and four at Marrara, Green delivered everything that he has promised, a third Test century and first on home soil.
There was some luck, Green didn't look good last night and was delivered some divine intervention when an inside edge onto his leg stump didn't produce a wicket, the bail held in place by some benevolent force far in excess of that provided by mere gravity.
But since that fortuitous slice of relief, Green made hay, playing the ball teasingly late from under his eyes, and with the balance and poise of a man who deserves to be batting in Test cricket.
It was his first Test century since he scored 174 not out against New Zealand in Wellington back in February 2024.
